sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: An **oscillation** is a repeated movement back and forth around **equilibrium**, the position where the system would rest. When the spring is stretched or squeezed, it pulls or pushes the mass back toward that resting position.
children: The mass has **inertia**, so it does not stop when it reaches equilibrium. It keeps going and displaces the spring on the other side.
The spring now acts in the opposite direction and brings the mass back again, and the cycle repeats.

teaching.text: The same mass can move in two directions.
children: In **longitudinal motion**, the mass travels along the line of the spring, so the spring itself gets longer and shorter.

In **transverse motion**, the mass travels across the spring line. The two spring segments are already pulled tight, and moving the mass above or below their resting line tilts their pull so that it points back toward the line.

teaching.text: The return comes from a force that keeps changing direction.
children: While the mass is on one side, the spring acts toward equilibrium from that side.
Once the mass crosses over, the displacement flips, and so does the restoring direction. The back-and-forth motion grows out of this repeated exchange between inertia and the restoring force.

teaching.text: Both pictures repeat at the same **frequency**, the number of cycles per second, which here is **0.5 Hz**.
children: They match because the mass and the total restoring stiffness are the same in both directions. Direction of motion alone does not set the rate.
The model has no damping, so the motion keeps going at full size instead of dying away.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: Two properties set how fast a mass on a spring oscillates, its **mass** and its **stiffness**. The demonstration runs three systems side by side and changes one property at a time.
children: The reference system has mass **m** and stiffness **K** and oscillates at **0.5 Hz**.
The heavier system has mass **4m** with the same stiffness and oscillates at **0.25 Hz**.
The stiffer system has the original mass with stiffness **4K** and oscillates at **1 Hz**.

teaching.text: **Greater mass lowers the frequency** when stiffness stays the same.
children: A heavier mass is harder to speed up, slow down and turn around.
The same restoring force therefore needs more time to finish each cycle, and four times the mass halves the rate.

teaching.text: **Greater stiffness raises the frequency** when mass stays the same.
children: A stiffer spring produces a stronger pull back toward equilibrium for the same displacement.
The mass turns around sooner and fits more cycles into the same time, and four times the stiffness doubles the rate.
Mass sets how strongly the system resists a change in motion, while stiffness sets how strongly it is pulled back.

teaching.text: Frequency is read by counting complete repetitions over the same stretch of time.
children: How far the mass travels is its **amplitude**, which is a separate property from its rate.

The longitudinal and transverse versions match in each row because their **effective restoring stiffness**, the restoring action in the actual direction of motion, is the same. Across the spring line, that stiffness comes from tension and geometry, so making a spring harder to stretch along its length does not automatically make it stiffer across it.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: Two equal masses joined by springs between two fixed ends have **two normal modes**. A **normal mode** is a coordinated pattern of motion in which every part repeats at one shared frequency and keeps the same relationship to the other parts.
children: The chain has three equal coupling springs, one between each fixed end and a mass and one in the middle.

teaching.text: In **Mode 1**, both masses move in the same direction at the same time.
children: The distance between them barely changes, so the middle spring is stretched and squeezed very little.
This is the slower pattern, at **0.4 Hz** in the demonstration.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the masses move toward and away from each other.
children: Now the middle spring is compressed and stretched strongly on every cycle.
That extra restoring force makes the pattern faster, at about **1.73 times** the Mode 1 frequency. It is faster without being exactly twice as fast.

teaching.text: A mode describes the whole system, not one mass.
children: Both masses take part in each mode, so one mass does not belong to Mode 1 while the other belongs to Mode 2.
The masses and springs stay the same in both patterns, and only their relationship changes.

teaching.text: The two modes can happen at the same time.
children: Their movements add together at each mass, reinforcing where they point the same way and partly or fully canceling where they point opposite ways. This adding is called **superposition**.

The bottom row of the demonstration is the exact sum of the two modes, so the combined motion contains both frequencies at once. The longitudinal and transverse chains follow the same relationships in different directions.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: Three equal masses between fixed ends have **three normal modes**, one for each movable mass. The chain has four equal coupling springs.
In **Mode 1**, all three masses move in the same direction.
children: The middle mass travels farthest, and the two outer masses travel less. Moving together does not require moving the same distance.
This is the slowest pattern, at **0.32 Hz** in the demonstration.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the two outer masses move in opposite directions while the middle mass stays at equilibrium.
children: The pulls on the middle mass from its two sides balance, so it does not move.
A point that stays still throughout a mode is called a **node**.
This pattern runs at about **1.85 times** the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: In **Mode 3**, the two outer masses move together while the middle mass moves against both of them.
children: Every neighbor now opposes its neighbor, so the springs between them change strongly.
This is the fastest pattern, at about **2.41 times** the lowest frequency.

teaching.text: The ordering follows how strongly neighboring masses oppose each other.
children: More opposition between neighbors means more spring stretching, which means a stronger restoring force and a faster pattern.

The same three masses take part in every mode, and no extra mass joins in at a higher mode. The colors track individual masses, and the resting marks give the position each displacement is measured from.

teaching.text: The frequency ratios belong to this particular chain and are not simple whole-number multiples.
children: When all three modes run together, their motions add at each mass.
The middle mass can still move in the mixture, because Modes 1 and 3 move it even though it is a node in Mode 2.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: Each movable mass adds one more **normal mode** in the direction being modeled. The atlas lines up chains with one through six masses, so they have one through six modes.
children: Each row is one chain, and each column is one mode number.
Smaller chains leave the later columns empty, because they have no such modes, which gives **21** patterns in all.
Every chain has equal masses, one more coupling spring than masses and two fixed ends.

teaching.text: Within a chain, **Mode 1** is the broadest pattern, with all the masses moving together.
children: Each higher mode adds another group moving in the opposite direction.
More reversals across the chain mean more places where neighbors pull against each other. The springs change more, the restoring force is stronger and the pattern repeats faster.

teaching.text: The fixed endpoints never move in any mode.
children: A mass that stays still inside one mode is a node of that pattern, but the rest of the chain is still moving.
A higher mode does not use smaller masses or stiffer springs. It uses the same parts arranged in a different relationship, and the mode number names the pattern, not any particular mass.

teaching.text: Colors mark the mode number and rows mark the number of masses.
children: Every pattern is scaled to the same largest displayed displacement, so the height of a picture says nothing about its frequency.
**Amplitude** is how far things move, and frequency is how often they repeat.
Chains of separate masses generally do not have the exact whole-number frequency spacing of an ideal continuous string.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** is held still at both ends, so both endpoints are **nodes**.
children: **Mode 1** fits one half-wave into the string’s length.
Modes 2 through 5 fit two, three, four and five half-waves.

teaching.text: More half-waves in the same length means a shorter wavelength.
children: At the same wave speed, a shorter wavelength repeats faster.

The five modes run at **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz**, which are consecutive **harmonics**, whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency, the **fundamental**. Both odd and even harmonics are present.

teaching.text: The same string can carry all five modes at once.
children: Their movements add at every point along the string, reinforcing in some places and canceling in others as their cycles shift.
The overall shape keeps changing even though each component stays perfectly regular.
A spot can look almost flat for a moment through cancellation and then move strongly a moment later. No component has been removed when that happens.

teaching.text: The playback is slowed by a factor of **250**, so 100 Hz is displayed at **0.4 Hz**.
children: Every mode is slowed by the same factor, which keeps their relative rates the same.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at a single point, **17%** of the way along the string, records the movement there.
children: Its **spectrum** puts frequency on one axis and amplitude on the other, and it has one peak for each of the five components.

The peaks are equal in height because each mode’s strength was chosen to give the same contribution at this pickup. At another position the heights would differ, so equal peaks do not mean equal motion everywhere.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface with fixed outer edges. Its modes are labeled with two numbers, which count the moving regions along the two directions of the surface.
children: **(1,1)** has one broad region moving up and down.
**(2,1)** and **(1,2)** split the surface into two regions, in different directions.
**(2,2)** makes four regions, and **(3,1)** makes three regions along one direction.
Neighboring regions move in opposite directions, and the lines between them are **nodes** that stay still.

teaching.text: The five modes add at every point of the surface.
children: Their contributions reinforce or cancel, producing one constantly changing shape.
The combined panel uses a smaller vertical scale than the single-mode panels, so heights cannot be compared directly across them.

teaching.text: A node stays still for the whole cycle of its mode.
children: A moving region also passes through the resting surface for an instant on every cycle, but that brief crossing does not make it a node.
Following one region as it rises, crosses rest and falls, while its neighbor does the opposite, separates the two.
The two numbers describe how the surface is divided. They are not two frequencies, two membranes or a count of elapsed cycles.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one marked point records the motion there, and its **spectrum** has one peak per mode.
children: The mode strengths were chosen to make the five peaks equal at that point.

The frequencies **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** were **assigned for the illustration**. They are not the natural resonances of this rectangle, so their even spacing teaches how frequencies combine without claiming that every membrane has harmonic spacing.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: The **scientific method** depends on stating very clear theories about how the world works, usually in the form of **differential equations**.
children: A differential equation describes how quantities in a system change.
Solving the equations gives a **prediction** of what we should find when we actually measure the world.

teaching.text: The theory here is that the **vocal folds are a membrane**.
children: When a membrane vibrates, the wave of vibration has **equidistant peaks** in its spectrum. These evenly spaced peaks are called **harmonics**.
The equations involved are like the spring and membrane equations already met, only somewhat more complicated.

teaching.text: The theory leads to a specific prediction.
children: If anyone’s **laryngeal vibration** signal is measured, its spectrum should have **equidistant harmonics**, peaks separated by equal frequency intervals.
The test is to record real vocal-fold vibration and examine its spectrum. Evenly spaced peaks would agree with the prediction, and a different pattern would challenge the model.

teaching.text: The prediction is more specific than just seeing vibration.
children: The vocal folds could vibrate without producing evenly spaced peaks, so the spectrum is what tests the theory.

The membrane animation used assigned harmonic frequencies, so it pictures what the idea looks like but does not test it. Only a recording of real vocal-fold vibration can do that, and the experiment is proposed here without a reported outcome.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** has one end held still and the other end free to move.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, a point of no movement.
The free end must be an **antinode**, the point of greatest movement over a cycle.

teaching.text: The allowed shapes fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves**.
children: The simplest mode fits one quarter-wave into the length.
The next modes fit three, five and seven quarter-waves.
These are the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**, so the second allowed mode is the third harmonic, not the second.

teaching.text: Only odd counts satisfy both endpoint conditions.
children: An even count of quarter-waves would put a node at the free end, which the free end does not allow.
Higher modes fit shorter wavelengths into the same length, so they repeat faster.

teaching.text: The demonstration uses **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**, slowed by a factor of **250** for display.
children: A spectrum taken at the free end has four equal peaks, because the modes were given equal strengths.
An antinode does not stay at its farthest point. It swings through rest to the other side while the fixed end stays still.
Counting allowed shapes and comparing frequencies answer different questions, even though both use numbers.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were **tuned separately** to the same fundamental.
children: If only the endpoint changed, with the same length and wave speed, the fundamental would drop to half.
Matching labels across the two examples therefore do not isolate the effect of the free end.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: A **dynamic system** is any system that changes over time because its parts keep influencing one another. The same way of thinking that explains a mass on a spring also appears in economics.
children: **Woodford’s theory** is called **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or **DSGE**.
“Dynamic” means the economy changes over time, “stochastic” means random shocks keep disturbing it, and “general equilibrium” means its many markets are linked and settle toward balance together.

teaching.text: The stabilization picture tracks two economic quantities over time.
children: The **black curve is unemployment**, and the **gray curve is inflation**.
At first both curves swing through large, jagged peaks and troughs.
After stabilization, the swings become smaller and smoother.

teaching.text: **Stabilization** means shrinking those swings.
children: It does not mean stopping all change, and it does not merge unemployment and inflation into a single quantity.
The aim is to avoid harmful extremes, such as very high unemployment or runaway inflation.

teaching.text: The link to physical systems is the shared question of what drives a fluctuation and what can damp it.
children: A spring system oscillates because of inertia and a restoring force.
An economy fluctuates because of shocks and the ways its parts respond to one another. The curves picture the goal of calmer swings without testing any particular policy.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Seven **principles of mass–spring systems** gather the main ideas into a short list.
The first principle is about the whole system.
children: **Raising the mass lowers the frequency**, because a heavier load is harder to turn around.
**Raising the stiffness raises the frequency**, because a stronger restoring force reverses the motion sooner.

teaching.text: The second principle counts modes.
children: A system with **n masses has n modes** of vibration.
Each mode has a higher frequency than the one before it.

teaching.text: The third, fourth and fifth principles say that **location matters**.
children: Added mass lowers a mode’s frequency in proportion to **how much the mass moves** in that mode, and that depends on where it sits.
Added stiffness raises a mode’s frequency in proportion to **how much the spring stretches or compresses** there, which also depends on position.

Where movement is greatest, there is no stretching, and where stretching is greatest, there is no movement. Neighbors that travel together do not change their spacing, so strong motion and strong compression fall in different places.

teaching.text: The same added mass can therefore matter a great deal in one mode and very little in another.
children: It matters where that mode moves strongly.
It matters little where that mode hardly moves, such as near a node. A node of one mode can still move in another mode or in a mixture.

teaching.text: The last two principles concern harmonics.
children: In a **fixed–fixed system**, the harmonics are whole-number multiples of the base frequency, because the base shape fits a whole number of times into each higher mode.
In a **fixed–free system**, the harmonics are **odd multiples** of the base frequency, because the base shape fits an odd number of times into each higher mode.

In **Mode 4**, the highlighted region moves strongly.
children: Neighboring points move nearly together, so the string barely stretches there.
In **Mode 5**, the same region barely moves, but neighboring points move differently, so the string stretches and compresses strongly there.

teaching.text: **Adding mass** to the region affects the two modes differently.

Mode 4 barely stretches the region, so the extra stiffness has little effect.

teaching.text: Increasing **both** mass and stiffness at that spot therefore **lowers Mode 4 and raises Mode 5**.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Seven **principles of mass–spring systems** gather the main ideas into a short list.
The first principle is about the whole system.

teaching.text: The second principle counts modes.

Each mode has a higher frequency than the one before it.

teaching.text: The third, fourth and fifth principles say that **location matters**.

Added stiffness raises a mode’s frequency in proportion to **how much the spring stretches or compresses** there, which also depends on position.

Where movement is greatest, there is no stretching, and where stretching is greatest, there is no movement. Neighbors that travel together do not change their spacing, so strong motion and strong compression fall in different places.

teaching.text: The same added mass can therefore matter a great deal in one mode and very little in another.
children: It matters where that mode moves strongly.

teaching.text: The last two principles concern harmonics.

teaching.text: Compression and movement work together like a spring and a mass.

children: When air is compressed, as it is in a constriction, it resists further compression more strongly.
A constriction placed where the air is **compressed a lot** therefore **raises the frequency**.

teaching.text: Narrowing also raises the air’s **mass**.
children: Bunching air up makes its density larger.
In a part of the tract where the air **moves a lot**, constricting adds moving mass, which tends to **lower the frequency**.

teaching.text: A constriction increases mass and stiffness together, but that does not mean their effects cancel.
children: The parts of a vibrating medium that **move the most** alternate with the parts that **compress and expand the most**.
Each mode places those regions differently.

teaching.text: Telling the two effects apart means following the air through a cycle.
children: Follow one air element to see how far it travels. That travel carries the local mass.
Compare it with its neighbors to see their gaps close and open. That spacing change is compression, the source of the restoring force.
A tongue-height label or a single frozen frame cannot give both pieces of information.

teaching.text: The same narrowing can work mainly through **mass** for one formant and mainly through **stiffness** for another.
children: That explains how one constriction can lower one formant and raise another.
Neither physical rule is reversed. Mass still lowers frequency where air moves, and stiffness still raises it where air compresses.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column

teaching.text: An air column has two kinds of local behavior, **movement** and **compression**.
children: **Movement** is how far an air element travels.
**Compression** is how the gaps between neighboring elements change. Smaller gaps mean compression, and wider gaps mean **rarefaction**, air that is more spread out.
Elements can travel together with almost no change in spacing, and neighbors can squeeze and spread strongly around an element that barely moves.

teaching.text: The rows of the animation separate the patterns of one air column.
children: The moving **Schwa** row is the uniform-tube reference.
The **F1, F2 and F3** rows show the first three resonance patterns of that same column.
The closed left end prevents movement, and the open right end allows it. Each higher mode fits more alternating regions of movement and compression into the tube.

teaching.text: Compression and movement work together like a spring and a mass.
children: Crowded air pushes back toward its usual spacing, which is the restoring response.
Moving air has inertia, so it keeps going while the restoring response changes.
Together they keep the air oscillating around its usual positions.

teaching.text: The two kinds of region are found in different places.
children: A region with large movement carries a lot of moving mass but is not where the air squeezes most.
A region with large spacing changes supplies strong restoring force even though its central element travels little.

teaching.text: Following one element over a cycle reveals its movement, and following the gaps beside it reveals compression.
children: Added mass matters most where movement is strong.
Added stiffness matters most where compression is strong.
These places differ from mode to mode, and the rows are separate resonances, not separate air streams.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air inside the vocal tract can be modeled as a chain of masses and springs.
children: Air has **inertia**, so air that is moving tends to keep moving.
Squeezing air raises its pressure, so compressed air pushes back. The spring-like links in the model stand for that restoring effect.
The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube. They oscillate around their usual places instead of flowing steadily from the glottis to the lips.

teaching.text: The tube is treated as **fixed–free**.
children: The **glottis**, the opening between the vocal folds, is the fixed end.
The open **lips** are the free end.

teaching.text: The two lowest patterns correspond to the first two formants.
children: **Mode 1 is F1-like**, the lowest resonance of the tube.
**Mode 2 is F2-like**, with one more reversal inside the tube.
In the ideal uniform tube, Mode 2 repeats **three times** as fast as Mode 1, as a fixed–free system requires. A change in tract shape can alter that simple ratio.

teaching.text: Each mode is a coordinated back-and-forth pattern of the whole air column.
children: F1 and F2 are not two separate air streams or two places where sound comes out.
At some places, neighboring elements move together and their gaps hardly change. At others, the gaps keep closing and opening.

teaching.text: Three markers locate the vowel constrictions along the tube.
children: **/a/** sits about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.
**/i/** sits about **two-thirds** of the way.
**/u/** sits at the **lips**.

Each marker is the same spot in both modes. Added mass matters where a mode moves strongly, and added springiness matters where it compresses strongly, so one narrowing can affect F1 and F2 differently.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: The **/u/ model** adds loading at the open lips, which is the **free end** of the air column. In the model, the lip elements are drawn larger to stand for greater **effective mass**.
children: The larger elements do not mean heavier air molecules.
They mean that more air has to be moved back and forth at that spot.

teaching.text: Both lowest modes move strongly at the free end.
children: In **Mode 1**, motion dominates at the lips.
In **Mode 2**, motion also dominates at the lips.

teaching.text: More moving mass is harder to speed up and reverse.
children: Where motion dominates, the extra load makes each cycle take longer.
Both modes slow down, so the result is **F1 down and F2 down** compared with the uniform tube.

teaching.text: The two rows compare the same lip location in two different resonance patterns.
children: Their inner arrangements differ, but both have strong movement at the lips.
The added load slows both without making their shapes or frequencies the same. F1 stays the lower resonance and F2 the higher one.
Each change is measured against its own uniform reference.

teaching.text: The shared direction comes from the role of the lip region in both modes.
children: It is not a rule that every constriction lowers every formant.
The air still moves back and forth around its usual positions, and the larger elements mark the load carried in that movement.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: The **/i/ constriction** sits near the front of the tract, about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips. The narrowing changes one physical region, but that region plays a different role in each mode.
In **Mode 1**, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there moves strongly in this mode.
The constriction adds effective moving mass, which is harder to reverse.
The cycle slows, so **F1 goes down**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **springiness dominates** at the same spot.
children: The air there is strongly compressed and expanded in this mode.
The constriction strengthens the spring-like restoring response.
The cycle speeds up, so **F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: The region itself does not move to a new place when the mode changes.
children: What changes is its job within each coordinated pattern.
Where neighbors move together, extra moving load matters most. Where neighbors keep squeezing together and pulling apart, the restoring response matters most.

teaching.text: The result is **lower F1 and higher F2** than the uniform tube.
children: The mass and spring effects do not simply cancel.

Each mode uses the narrowed region differently, so one constriction pushes the two formants in opposite directions. The two arrows summarize two separate causes, slower movement from added mass and faster return from added springiness.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: The **/a/ constriction** sits farther back, about **one-third** of the way from the glottis to the lips. It changes a different part of each mode than the /i/ narrowing, while mass and stiffness keep their usual effects.
In **Mode 1**, **springiness dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there is strongly compressed in this mode.
The constriction adds restoring force, so the cycle speeds up and **F1 goes up**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there moves strongly in this mode.
The constriction adds effective moving mass, which is harder to reverse, so the cycle slows and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: The narrowing is in the same back location in both rows, but the rows are different coordinated motions of the air.
children: A region can move very little itself while its neighbors squeeze together and spread apart around it.
A region can also move a lot while its spacing barely changes.
Those two roles explain why springiness wins in Mode 1 and moving mass wins in Mode 2 at this spot.

teaching.text: The result is **higher F1 and lower F2**, the reverse of /i/.
children: Moving the constriction changes which role matters most. It does not change what mass or stiffness does.
The arrows give the direction of each change predicted by the model, not a measured size.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: **Source–filter theory** separates the sound made by the vocal folds from the way the vocal tract shapes it.
children: The **source** is the glottal vibration.
The **filter** is the vocal tract.

teaching.text: The glottal source gives a **harmonic comb**.
children: It repeats at a **fundamental frequency**, **F0**, and has harmonics at whole-number multiples of F0.
In the example, the harmonics are **100 Hz** apart and extend to **4000 Hz**.
Before the vocal tract acts, the source looks like evenly spaced vertical lines of equal height. Equal heights keep the example simple.

teaching.text: The vocal tract filter **sculpts the heights** of those harmonics.
children: Harmonics near the tract’s resonances, the **formants**, become stronger, and others become weaker.
The positions of the lines do not move. Only their heights change.
The broad outline of the heights is the **spectral envelope**, and the envelope is the vowel.

teaching.text: The schwa example labels four resonance regions, **F1 through F4**.
children: Its strongest group of harmonics sits at low frequency.

teaching.text: The spectrum puts frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis.
children: A taller line is stronger, not higher in frequency.
**F0** belongs to the source, and **F1** is the lowest resonance of the tract.
The vowel still contains many harmonics, not just four tones, and the resonance values describe this one example rather than every speaker.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: The **/i/ filter** has a **low F1** and a **high F2**. The same 100 Hz harmonic comb from the source passes through it.
children: The first strong group of harmonics sits near the low-frequency end.
The next strong group sits much farther up, with a weak region in between.
Further strong groups appear around **F3** and **F4**, near **3000** and **3600 Hz**.

teaching.text: The source harmonics stay in the same evenly spaced positions.
children: Only their heights change when the tract changes shape.
That makes the filter’s effect visible separately from the repetition of the source.

teaching.text: The low-F1, high-F2 pattern matches the front constriction of /i/.
children: The narrowing near two-thirds of the way from the glottis adds mass where Mode 1 moves and stiffness where Mode 2 compresses.
F1 falls and F2 rises, which spreads the two lowest formants far apart.

teaching.text: Reading the spectrum takes two separate judgments.
children: A line’s horizontal position gives its **frequency**.
A line’s height gives its **amplitude**.
A tall line near the low end is still low in frequency, even if a higher line is weaker.

teaching.text: The narrow harmonic lines sample the broad formant regions.
children: Each line is a source component, and the envelope traced by their heights is the vowel.
These values describe one schematic /i/, not an identical pattern for every speaker.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: Compared with /i/, the **/a/ filter** has a **higher F1** and a **lower F2**. In the example, **F1 is at 750 Hz** and **F2 is near 1200 Hz**, so the first two resonance regions sit close together.
children: **F3** and **F4** stay higher, near **2600** and **3500 Hz**.
The same evenly spaced source produces a different vowel because the tract changed shape.

teaching.text: The filter changes the pattern of harmonic **strengths**.
children: Moving a formant shifts which frequency region is favored, a change along the horizontal axis.
Changing a harmonic’s amplitude changes its height, a change along the vertical axis.
These are two different kinds of change in the spectrum.

teaching.text: A formant can fall **between two source harmonics**.
children: The 750 Hz target for F1 lies between the harmonics at **700** and **800 Hz**.
The nearby harmonics become stronger, but no new source line appears exactly at 750 Hz.

teaching.text: A formant and a harmonic are different things.
children: A **formant** names a resonance region of the tract, the filter.
A **harmonic** names a frequency component of the repeating source.
The drawing’s values belong to this simplified comparison.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: A **spectrum** and a **spectrogram** show the same sound in two different ways.
A **spectrum** is **one instant**.
children: It describes the frequency components in one short slice of sound.
Frequency runs horizontally and amplitude vertically.
The example takes three spectra from **/i/** and three from **/a/**.

teaching.text: A **spectrogram** **stacks many spectra over time**.
children: Time runs from left to right, and frequency runs upward.
The first step turns the spectrum’s frequency axis on its side, so a peak near the right of a spectrum becomes a mark higher up in the spectrogram.
Moving to the right in a spectrogram means later in time, not higher in frequency.

teaching.text: The second step turns **spectrum height into darkness**.
children: In the grayscale display, **black means high amplitude, gray means medium and white means low**.
Vertical position gives frequency, and darkness gives strength.
A band that darkens is getting stronger, while a band that rises is moving to a higher frequency.

teaching.text: During the change from **/i/** to **/a/**, **F1 rises and F2 falls**.
children: The two lowest bands move toward each other.
The higher bands stay above them with smaller changes.
The spectrogram follows the changing resonances of the tract through time.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: Formants are easiest to see when the source harmonics are **closely spaced**. Each harmonic acts as a sample of the vocal tract’s response, and many samples trace the shape of each formant clearly.
With harmonics at **100, 200, 300, 400 Hz** and so on, a vowel with **F1 at 300** and **F2 at 2100 Hz** shapes the amplitudes of many harmonics.
children: Many lines fall around each formant.
Their heights rise and fall with the filter, so the formant regions are easy to pick out.

teaching.text: Raising **F0** spreads the harmonics apart.
children: With harmonics at **250, 500, 750** and so on, fewer lines fall near each formant.
A formant can land between two harmonics, so no line sits at its center.
One strong line may be near a formant without marking its exact location. It becomes very hard to tell harmonics from formants.

teaching.text: Higher voices make the problem worse.
children: A **toddler’s** harmonics could be **400, 800** and so on.
A **soprano’s** could be **800, 1600, 2400** and so on.
The three spectra and their spectrograms move from closely spaced components to a few isolated traces.

teaching.text: The tract has not lost or moved its resonances.
children: The filter can stay exactly the same.
What changed is the source, which now supplies fewer frequencies to reveal that same filter.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface with fixed outer edges. Its modes are labeled with two numbers, which count the moving regions along the two directions of the surface.
children: **(1,1)** has one broad region moving up and down.
**(2,1)** and **(1,2)** split the surface into two regions, in different directions.
**(2,2)** makes four regions, and **(3,1)** makes three regions along one direction.
Neighboring regions move in opposite directions, and the lines between them are **nodes** that stay still.

teaching.text: The five modes add at every point of the surface.
children: Their contributions reinforce or cancel, producing one constantly changing shape.
The combined panel uses a smaller vertical scale than the single-mode panels, so heights cannot be compared directly across them.

teaching.text: A node stays still for the whole cycle of its mode.
children: A moving region also passes through the resting surface for an instant on every cycle, but that brief crossing does not make it a node.
Following one region as it rises, crosses rest and falls, while its neighbor does the opposite, separates the two.
The two numbers describe how the surface is divided. They are not two frequencies, two membranes or a count of elapsed cycles.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one marked point records the motion there, and its **spectrum** has one peak per mode.
children: The mode strengths were chosen to make the five peaks equal at that point.

The frequencies **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** were **assigned for the illustration**. They are not the natural resonances of this rectangle, so their even spacing teaches how frequencies combine without claiming that every membrane has harmonic spacing.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–free system** has one end held still and the other end free to move.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, a point of no movement.
The free end must be an **antinode**, the point of greatest movement over a cycle.

teaching.text: The allowed shapes fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves**.
children: The simplest mode fits one quarter-wave into the length.
The next modes fit three, five and seven quarter-waves.
These are the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**, so the second allowed mode is the third harmonic, not the second.

teaching.text: Only odd counts satisfy both endpoint conditions.
children: An even count of quarter-waves would put a node at the free end, which the free end does not allow.
Higher modes fit shorter wavelengths into the same length, so they repeat faster.

teaching.text: The demonstration uses **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**, slowed by a factor of **250** for display.
children: A spectrum taken at the free end has four equal peaks, because the modes were given equal strengths.
An antinode does not stay at its farthest point. It swings through rest to the other side while the fixed end stays still.
Counting allowed shapes and comparing frequencies answer different questions, even though both use numbers.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were **tuned separately** to the same fundamental.
children: If only the endpoint changed, with the same length and wave speed, the fundamental would drop to half.
Matching labels across the two examples therefore do not isolate the effect of the free end.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: A **quarter-wavelength** is the piece of a standing wave that connects a **node** to an **antinode**. On the fixed–free string, the fixed bottom must be a node and the free top must be an antinode.
children: **One quarter-wave** fits exactly between them.
It gives the simplest allowed pattern, with no still point inside the string.

teaching.text: The next pattern cannot add just one more quarter-wave.
children: One more would end the string at a node.
A node is the wrong condition for the free top.

teaching.text: Adding **two** quarter-waves keeps an antinode at the top.
children: The allowed patterns therefore fit **one, three, five and seven quarter-waves** into the same length.
More sections in the same length mean shorter wavelengths.
At the same wave speed, shorter waves repeat faster, so each pattern has a higher frequency than the last.

teaching.text: The demonstration reveals one quarter-wave packet at a time in every mode that contains it.
children: The four modes contain **1, 3, 5 and 7** packets, matching the odd harmonics.
The numbered pieces divide the standing shape. They do not move up the string one after another.
The string moves back and forth while the still points of the pattern stay in place.

teaching.text: The odd frequency pattern follows from the two endpoint conditions.
children: Even frequencies are missing because no even count of quarter-waves can end on an antinode at the free top.
Nothing has been chosen arbitrarily, since the boundaries themselves rule those patterns out.

teaching.text: **Modes 1, 2 and 3** arrange these regions differently along the tube.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: **Mode 1** and **Mode 2** are two resonance patterns of the same air column. The glottal end is held, and the lips are open.
children: Both modes move the air strongly near the lips.
Mode 2 has one more reversal inside the tube, so its movement and compression are arranged differently.

teaching.text: Three markers sit at the **back**, the **front** and the **lips**.
children: Each marker is the same physical place in both modes.
Narrowing the tract at one marker changes that region for both modes at once.

teaching.text: The effect of the narrowing depends on what each mode is doing at that marker.

teaching.text: The **/u/ model** adds loading at the open lips, which is the **free end** of the air column. In the model, the lip elements are drawn larger to stand for greater **effective mass**.

teaching.text: Both lowest modes move strongly at the free end.
children: In **Mode 1**, motion dominates at the lips.
In **Mode 2**, motion also dominates at the lips.

teaching.text: More moving mass is harder to speed up and reverse.
children: Where motion dominates, the extra load makes each cycle take longer.
Both modes slow down, so the result is **F1 down and F2 down** compared with the uniform tube.

teaching.text: The two rows compare the same lip location in two different resonance patterns.
children: Their inner arrangements differ, but both have strong movement at the lips.
The added load slows both without making their shapes or frequencies the same. F1 stays the lower resonance and F2 the higher one.
Each change is measured against its own uniform reference.

teaching.text: The shared direction comes from the role of the lip region in both modes.
children: It is not a rule that every constriction lowers every formant.
The air still moves back and forth around its usual positions, and the larger elements mark the load carried in that movement.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: The **/i/ constriction** sits near the front of the tract, about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips. The narrowing changes one physical region, but that region plays a different role in each mode.
In **Mode 1**, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there moves strongly in this mode.
The constriction adds effective moving mass, which is harder to reverse.
The cycle slows, so **F1 goes down**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **springiness dominates** at the same spot.
children: The air there is strongly compressed and expanded in this mode.
The constriction strengthens the spring-like restoring response.
The cycle speeds up, so **F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: The region itself does not move to a new place when the mode changes.
children: What changes is its job within each coordinated pattern.
Where neighbors move together, extra moving load matters most. Where neighbors keep squeezing together and pulling apart, the restoring response matters most.

teaching.text: The result is **lower F1 and higher F2** than the uniform tube.
children: The mass and spring effects do not simply cancel.

Each mode uses the narrowed region differently, so one constriction pushes the two formants in opposite directions. The two arrows summarize two separate causes, slower movement from added mass and faster return from added springiness.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: The **/a/ constriction** sits farther back, about **one-third** of the way from the glottis to the lips. It changes a different part of each mode than the /i/ narrowing, while mass and stiffness keep their usual effects.
In **Mode 1**, **springiness dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there is strongly compressed in this mode.
The constriction adds restoring force, so the cycle speeds up and **F1 goes up**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **mass motion dominates** at the narrowing.
children: The air there moves strongly in this mode.
The constriction adds effective moving mass, which is harder to reverse, so the cycle slows and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: The narrowing is in the same back location in both rows, but the rows are different coordinated motions of the air.
children: A region can move very little itself while its neighbors squeeze together and spread apart around it.
A region can also move a lot while its spacing barely changes.
Those two roles explain why springiness wins in Mode 1 and moving mass wins in Mode 2 at this spot.

teaching.text: The result is **higher F1 and lower F2**, the reverse of /i/.
children: Moving the constriction changes which role matters most. It does not change what mass or stiffness does.
The arrows give the direction of each change predicted by the model, not a measured size.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: An air column has two kinds of local behavior, **movement** and **compression**.
children: **Movement** is how far an air element travels.
**Compression** is how the gaps between neighboring elements change. Smaller gaps mean compression, and wider gaps mean **rarefaction**, air that is more spread out.
Elements can travel together with almost no change in spacing, and neighbors can squeeze and spread strongly around an element that barely moves.

teaching.text: The rows of the animation separate the patterns of one air column.
children: The moving **Schwa** row is the uniform-tube reference.
The **F1, F2 and F3** rows show the first three resonance patterns of that same column.
The closed left end prevents movement, and the open right end allows it. Each higher mode fits more alternating regions of movement and compression into the tube.

teaching.text: Compression and movement work together like a spring and a mass.
children: Crowded air pushes back toward its usual spacing, which is the restoring response.
Moving air has inertia, so it keeps going while the restoring response changes.
Together they keep the air oscillating around its usual positions.

teaching.text: The two kinds of region are found in different places.
children: A region with large movement carries a lot of moving mass but is not where the air squeezes most.
A region with large spacing changes supplies strong restoring force even though its central element travels little.

teaching.text: Following one element over a cycle reveals its movement, and following the gaps beside it reveals compression.
children: Added mass matters most where movement is strong.
Added stiffness matters most where compression is strong.
These places differ from mode to mode, and the rows are separate resonances, not separate air streams.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The vocal folds supply the voiced **source**. Their repetition rate is **F0**, and F0 sets the spacing between the harmonic lines in the source spectrum.
The top row recalls the **fixed–fixed membrane**, with five modes and their sum.
children: A pickup point records the combined motion.
These membrane frequencies were assigned for the illustration, not calculated as the natural resonances of every membrane.

teaching.text: The bottom row has **three source spectra** before the vocal tract filters them, all in the same **0 to 4000 Hz** window.
children: With **F0 at 100 Hz**, the harmonic lines are packed closely together.
With **F0 at 250 Hz**, the harmonics fall at **250, 500, 750** and onward, from **tighter, lighter vocal folds**.
With **F0 at 350 Hz**, they fall at **350, 700, 1050** and onward, from **very tight and light vocal folds**.

teaching.text: A lower F0 gives **denser harmonic sampling**, and a higher F0 gives **sparser sampling**.
children: The same window holds fewer lines as F0 rises.
Heavier, looser folds repeat more slowly, and lighter, tighter folds repeat faster. Mass resists changes in movement, and tension supplies the return.

teaching.text: A voiced vowel contains **many frequencies** at once.
children: Source repetition decides which harmonics are available.
The vocal tract then strengthens some regions and weakens others.
Changing pitch changes the source spacing, while changing vowel shape changes the tract’s favored regions. These are two separate contributions to one sound.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The **filter** is the vocal tract, modeled as a **fixed–free** tube with one end closed and one end open. It selects **formants**, and its core rule is simple.
children: A formant **encourages the closest harmonics to be audible**.
**Harmonics far from that formant are muted.**
The voiced source supplies the harmonics, and the filter chooses which ones survive. The vowel shape is the filter.

teaching.text: Each vowel places its formants differently.
children: **Schwa** has separate first and second resonances, near **500** and **1500 Hz**.
**/u/** places both lower, near **300** and **1000 Hz**, and also marks a third formant near **2000 Hz**.
The front vowel **/i/ or /ɪ/** has a low F1 near **300 Hz** and a much higher F2 near **2200 Hz**.
**/a/** places its first two targets close together, at **800** and **900 Hz**. These values belong to this illustration.

teaching.text: Changing the tongue and lips changes these favored frequency regions.
children: Each formant target pulls up the harmonics nearest to it.
Harmonics between targets stay weak.

teaching.text: A formant target and a harmonic line are different things.
children: The **target** identifies a resonance of the tract.
The **line** identifies a component of the source.
A target can sit between two lines and still strengthen the harmonics on either side. Filtering changes heights without creating a new component exactly at each target.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: The grid crosses **source** rows with **vowel filter** columns, so the same filter can be compared at different pitches. **Dashed red ticks** mark the formant targets, and **colored stems** mark the actual harmonics after filtering.
Each row keeps the source fixed.
children: The top row comes from **heavy, loose** vocal folds, with closely spaced harmonics.
The middle row comes from **lighter, tighter** folds with **F0 at 250 Hz**.
The bottom row comes from the **lightest, tightest** folds with **F0 at 350 Hz**.

teaching.text: Each column keeps the vowel filter fixed.
children: Moving down a column changes only F0.
Moving across a row changes only the vowel filter.
These two directions separate the effects of the source from the effects of tract shape.

teaching.text: **Dense harmonics trace the formant shape well.**
children: With a low F0, many harmonics fall near each resonance.
Their heights describe the filter’s **envelope**, the smooth outline of favored strengths.
More harmonics in the window give a smoother, easier-to-read spectrum.

teaching.text: **Sparse harmonics can miss a formant or make it look ambiguous.**
children: A higher F0 leaves wider gaps between the stems.
A strong stem may sit beside a formant target instead of on it, even though the target has not moved.
The two close /a/ targets can then look like one grouped region.

teaching.text: Difficulty reading a formant does not mean the resonance disappeared.
children: The ticks stay in the same place in each column.
When the targets are unchanged but the stems spread apart, the source has changed and the filter has not.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrum** is **one instant**, and a **spectrogram** **stacks many spectra over time**.
children: In a spectrum, frequency runs horizontally, and peak height gives amplitude for one short slice of sound.
The sequence contains three slices of **/i/** followed by three slices of **/a/**.

teaching.text: The first step maps the spectrum’s frequency axis onto the spectrogram’s **vertical axis**.
children: The slices are then placed from left to right in time.
Frequency now runs upward.

teaching.text: The second step turns **spectrum height into darkness**.
children: **Black** means high amplitude, **gray** means medium and **white** means low.
A rising band is moving to a higher frequency.
A darkening band is getting stronger at the frequency where it already is.

teaching.text: The two displays use the horizontal axis for different things.
children: Moving right in a spectrum means a higher frequency.
Moving right in a spectrogram means a later time.

teaching.text: During the **/i/ to /a/** transition, the first strong band **rises** and the second strong band **falls**.
children: One upper band also moves down, while a fainter band stays in the high-frequency region.
Connecting neighboring slices traces how the resonance pattern changes.
Position and darkness carry different information about that change.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Speech-complexity experiment prompt
Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: Speech science now leads **back to AI**. The plan is to build a **neural network** that is trained on students’ own **formants** and decides which vowel is being spoken.
The network’s inputs are **F1** and **F2**.
children: F1 and F2 are the first two resonance regions that the vocal tract emphasizes.
They give a compact pair of measurements for each vowel instead of every point in the waveform.

teaching.text: The **input** and the **output** carry different kinds of information.
children: The input is a pair of measurements of the sound.
The intended output picks out one of the candidate vowel categories.
The formant pair supplies evidence about the sound, and the true label tells which category an example belongs to. Recognition means relating the measured pattern to the right category.

teaching.text: The exercise links the physics of speech with machine learning.
children: The mass–spring account explains where F1 and F2 come from.
The network learns how those two numbers relate to vowel categories.
At this stage, the inputs and the task are defined. Whether the network recognizes vowels well is a question for training and testing.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: A **purely linear network** takes **2 inputs** through **hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons** to **5 outputs**, with **no activation functions**.
children: The two inputs are **F1** and **F2**, and their order keeps their meanings straight.

teaching.text: Every layer is **fully connected**.
children: Each receiving neuron connects to every neuron in the layer before it.
Each connection carries a **weight**.
A receiving neuron multiplies each incoming value by its weight and adds up the products.

teaching.text: The hidden layers hold intermediate combinations.
children: The first hidden layer has **three** neurons, the second has **two** and the third has **four**.
Hidden values are new combinations of the inputs. They are not new measured formants, and they are not finished categories.
Different weights let neurons combine the same inputs in different ways.

teaching.text: The five outputs stand for five words.
children: From top to bottom, they are **/done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/** and **/Dan/**.
Keeping that order fixed keeps the meaning of each output value.

teaching.text: **Purely linear** means each layer passes on its weighted sums with no activation function in between.
children: The computation is a chain of weighted sums.
Passing sums forward describes the computation, but it does not by itself make the final five values into probabilities.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: An example input enters the network, **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**. **Every edge gets a random weight.**
children: The inputs are measurements of the sound.
The **weights** are settings that decide how the network combines those measurements.
Changing the weights changes the internal results even when the input pair stays the same.

teaching.text: Each connection supplies one weight.
children: A neuron multiplies its incoming values by their weights and adds the products.
A neuron in the first hidden layer receives F1 and F2, so it has two incoming weights.
The three neurons there can form three different combinations of the same pair.

teaching.text: Before training, **every weight is a random number between −1 and 1**.
children: Values such as **0.95**, **−0.91** and **0.28** appear on the edges.

The heading says **blue for positive** and **orange for negative**, though the negative edges appear green in the rendered figure. The written signs give the direction, and the sizes give the strength.
Positive and negative contributions can reinforce or oppose one another.

teaching.text: These are **random starting values**, not learned knowledge about vowels.
children: A **forward pass** processes an example using whatever weights are current.
**Learning** is the process that changes those weights.
Naming the outputs does not mean the starting network recognizes their categories correctly.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: In the **forward flow**, the input moves forward **layer by layer**. At the output, the network gives **a distribution over the five words**.
children: The animation carries the input pair along the connections from one layer to the next.
Each layer combines the values from the layer before it using the current weights.

teaching.text: The illustrated output assigns probabilities to the five words.
children: **/dune/**, **/dean/** and **/Don/** get **0.1** each.
/done/ is the favored prediction, while the other words keep some support.

teaching.text: A valid probability distribution has two properties.
children: Every value lies between zero and one.
The values add up to one, and these five do.

teaching.text: These bars illustrate the intended kind of output.
children: The purely linear network has no step that guarantees a probability distribution.
So the bars picture the goal rather than a verified result of the shown weights.

teaching.text: The **predicted category** and the **true category** are different.
children: The predicted category is the one the model favors.
The true category is the example’s actual label.
Judging whether the prediction is right requires that true label. The tallest bar and the smiley face alone cannot supply it.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: The same network can be written in **PyTorch**.
children: **import torch** loads the library.
**import torch.nn as nn** loads its neural-network tools under the short name **nn**.
The model is assigned to the variable **net**.

teaching.text: **nn.Sequential** stacks the layers in the order that information passes through them.
children: The comment marks the shape as purely linear, **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**.
Each **nn.Linear** layer produces weighted sums of its incoming values.

teaching.text: The four layers match the picture.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False)** takes 2 inputs to 3 outputs.
**nn.Linear(3, 2, bias=False)** takes 3 to 2.
**nn.Linear(2, 4, bias=False)** takes 2 to 4.
**nn.Linear(4, 5, bias=False)** takes 4 to 5.
Each layer’s output count matches the next layer’s input count, which lets information flow through. The final five values match the five candidate words.

teaching.text: **nn.Linear(in, out)** holds an **out × in weight matrix**, one weight per connection.
children: **bias=False** removes the extra constant that a layer could add to each weighted sum.
It keeps every layer a **pure linear map**, as in the picture, while keeping all the weights and the ability to learn them.

teaching.text: This is a **declaration only, with no training**.
children: No activation layers appear, so the whole sequence stays linear.
Declaring the structure does not train it or produce the probability bars. Training requires examples and a process for changing the weights.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: The vowel network takes two formant measurements, **F1** and **F2**, and gives one response for each of five words, **done, dune, dean, Don** and **Dan**, in that order.
children: The inputs carry measurements of the sound.
The outputs carry the network’s response for each possible word.
Both are drawn as circles, but they do different jobs.

teaching.text: Three **hidden layers** sit between the inputs and the outputs.
children: They contain **three, two and four** neurons.
The whole arrangement runs **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**. These numbers count the neurons in each layer, not recordings or training trials.
A hidden neuron receives values from the layer before it and sends its result to the layer after it.

teaching.text: The network is **fully connected**.
children: Every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next.
Each connection has its own **weight**, and all **40** illustrative weights are revealed, values such as **+0.005**, **−0.001**, **+0.6** and **−0.4**.
A weight sets how the value traveling along that connection contributes to the receiving neuron. A positive weight keeps the sign of the contribution, and a negative weight reverses it.

teaching.text: F1 reaches all three neurons in the first hidden layer, and so does F2.
children: Each of those connections has a different weight.
So each first-layer neuron combines the same two measurements in its own way.

teaching.text: The weights stay fixed for this network.
children: Changing a formant changes what travels through the connections.
Changing a weight changes how strongly a connection contributes.
A weight describes one connection’s contribution, not the probability of any word.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries information from the inputs, through the hidden layers, to the outputs. The example input is **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**.
The top neuron of the first hidden layer computes **w₁ times F1 plus w₂ times F2**.
children: Its weights are **+0.005** for F1 and **−0.001** for F2.
F1 contributes +0.005 times 320, and F2 contributes −0.001 times 2000.
Adding the positive and negative contributions gives **−0.40**.

teaching.text: Multiplying each input by its weight and adding the products is an **inner product**.
children: The other two neurons in that layer use the same inputs with different weights, giving **6.64** and **2.72**.
A negative result such as −0.40 is still a value the next layer can use.

teaching.text: Each later layer repeats the same operation on the values from the layer before it.
children: The second hidden layer gives about **5.50** and **−5.93**.
The third hidden layer gives about **1.57, −1.95, −1.95** and **−2.88**.
Values must flow in this order, because each neuron needs the results of the layer before it.

teaching.text: The five final weighted sums are **logits**, scores that are not yet probabilities.
children: **Softmax** turns them into probabilities. It raises e to each logit and divides by the sum of all five of those exponentials, so the five probabilities share one total of 1.
A negative logit still becomes a positive probability.

teaching.text: **Done** gets the largest probability, about **55.7%**, **Don** gets about 18.5%, **Dan** about 10.2%, **dean** about **8.1%** and **dune** about 7.4%.
children: These are the network’s current responses to this input. They do not say which word was actually spoken.
The hidden activations here are linear, and the weights stay fixed during the forward pass.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** starts by comparing what the network produced with what it should have produced.
children: The **computed output** is the current probability distribution, with **done** at **55.7%** and **dean** at only **8.1%**.
The **desired output** puts a **1** on **dean** and a **0** on the other four words, because dean is the word that was spoken.
The target names the correct word, so it can disagree with the network’s largest response.

teaching.text: **Cross-entropy loss** measures the mismatch using the probability given to the true word.
children: For this example, the loss is the negative log of the probability of dean.
Giving dean more probability lowers the loss, and giving it less raises it.

teaching.text: The calculation runs **backward**, from the output connections toward the inputs.
children: The contribution of the final layer of weights is found first.
That result is then used to find the contributions of hidden layer 3, then hidden layer 2 and finally hidden layer 1.
The four steps replace each layer’s weights with updated values, such as **+0.1** becoming **+0.083** and **+0.6** becoming **+0.622**.

teaching.text: A **gradient** describes how the loss changes when one weight changes slightly.
children: The update rule subtracts the learning rate, **η**, times the gradient from the old weight.
A positive gradient lowers the weight, and a negative gradient raises it. Learning does not simply make positive weights bigger or negative weights smaller.

teaching.text: The activations stored during the forward pass stay fixed throughout the backward pass.
children: All gradients use the original weights and stored activations, so together they form one simultaneous update.
A new forward pass is needed to see the updated network’s predictions.
The input connections use a much smaller learning rate because their inputs are raw formant values in hertz.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: The question is simple to state. **If we increase this w, will the error go up or down?**
children: The desired word is **dean**.
The network currently gives its largest probability to **done**.
What matters is how a small change in a weight affects the probability given to the true word.

teaching.text: The **pink-marked** connection runs from the top neuron of the last hidden layer to **done**.
children: It is a positive connection, and that hidden neuron has a positive activation of about **1.57**.
Increasing this weight raises done’s final score.
Softmax makes the five probabilities share one total, so boosting the wrong word leaves less probability for dean. The loss goes **up**.

teaching.text: The **blue-marked** connection runs from **F1** to the top neuron of the first hidden layer.
children: Increasing it raises that neuron’s value, because F1 is positive.
That change then travels through several positive and negative connections and reaches all five outputs.
The sign of this first connection alone cannot decide whether the error rises or falls.

teaching.text: The full backward calculation settles it for this network and the dean target.
children: The gradient for the input connection is positive too.
A small increase therefore raises the error, so the update decreases this weight.
Both marked connections call for decreases here, but the early one needed the combined effect of every downstream path to establish that direction.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: Why does training **backpropagate**? Comparing the **last** weights with the **first** weights answers the question.
The **last weights, W5**, directly determine the output probabilities.
children: The error is very directly determined by them.
The difference between the computed and desired outputs can be used straight away to find better W5 values.

teaching.text: The **first weights, W2**, are much harder to judge.
children: W2 affects the first hidden activations.
Those activations affect two more layers of activations, along with other weights, before any output appears.
It is really hard to work out how much W2 is to blame for a mistake made all the way at the end.
The effect of W2 on the error **includes** the effect of W5, since W5 is downstream of W2.

teaching.text: So improving **W5 is the easy problem**, and improving W2 depends on it.
children: Solving small problems first and reusing their answers for bigger problems that depend on them is **dynamic programming**.
**Backpropagation is Bellman–Viterbi dynamic programming.**
It computes the effects near the output first and reuses them for each earlier layer, instead of redoing the whole downstream calculation for every early weight.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation = SGD + dynamic programming.**
children: **SGD**, stochastic gradient descent, is the rule that adjusts the weights.
Backpropagation supplies the gradients that rule needs, and dynamic programming makes computing them efficient.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: Training uses two **training matrices**, one of inputs and one of correct answers.
The **Formant_Inputs** matrix is **110 × 2**.
children: Each of its 110 rows holds **F1** and **F2** for one recording, in hertz.
The two columns are the two sound measurements, and the network takes one row at a time as one example.

teaching.text: The **TrueVowel_Outputs** matrix is **110 × 5**.
children: Its columns are **done, dune, dean, Don** and **Dan**.
Each row puts a **1** in the correct word’s column and **0** in the other four.
This is a **one-hot** target, since exactly one position is on.

teaching.text: The illustrative rows pair formants with words.
children: **500, 1500** goes with **done**.
**350, 1000** goes with **dune**.
**320, 2000** goes with **dean**, the same example used in the network.
**700, 1100** goes with **Don**, and **800, 1700** goes with **Dan**.

teaching.text: The rows of the two matrices must stay matched.
children: The third input row, 320 and 2000, pairs with the third target row, dean.
Moving an input row without moving its target would attach the measurements to the wrong answer.
The five shown rows illustrate the layout of the full 110 examples.

teaching.text: The network’s output is separate from the target matrix.
children: Before backpropagation, the network still favors **done** at 55.7% for the dean example.
The target keeps the correct label even when the network is wrong, and training compares the two.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: One full-batch training step can be written in a short **PyTorch** program.
The data are loaded first.
children: **X = torch.load("Formant_Inputs.pt").float()** loads the 110 × 2 formant matrix.
**Y = torch.load("TrueVowel_Outputs.pt").float()** loads the 110 × 5 one-hot targets.
**.float()** makes both into floating-point tensors. The program assumes these files already exist.

teaching.text: The network is declared with **nn.Sequential**.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, **nn.Linear(3, 2)**, **nn.Linear(2, 4)** and **nn.Linear(4, 5)** keep the **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5** arrangement.
No activation function is declared between the layers.

teaching.text: The training step has five lines.
children: **sgd = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=0.1)** sets up stochastic gradient descent with a **learning rate of 0.1**.
**sgd.zero_grad()** clears any gradients left from before.
**loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(net(X), Y)** runs the forward pass and compares the scores with Y. CrossEntropyLoss handles the softmax-related step itself, so the last layer supplies logits.
**loss.backward()** computes the gradient of the loss for every parameter.
**sgd.step()** changes the parameters using those gradients.

teaching.text: These steps are separate.
children: Computing a gradient does not change a weight by itself, and clearing gradients does not erase learned weights.
All **110 rows** contribute to this one step, and there is no repeated training loop.
The code uses PyTorch’s default starting weights and biases, so it shares the drawing’s layer sizes but not its exact numbers.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: The **sigmoid activation function** is **σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z))**. It takes an inner product, z, and returns a value between 0 and 1.
The sigmoid squashes large values toward its two limits.
children: If the inner product is a **large positive** number, the sigmoid is near **1**.
If it is a **large negative** number, the sigmoid is basically **0**.

teaching.text: The curve is S-shaped.
children: The horizontal axis is the **linear activation**, the weighted sum, and the vertical axis is the **sigmoid activation**.
The curve is steep in the middle and flat near both ends.
Near the ends, further changes in the input make only small changes in the output.

teaching.text: In the formula, a large positive z makes exp(−z) tiny, so the output approaches 1.
children: A large negative z makes exp(−z) huge, so the output approaches 0.

teaching.text: **Lord Edgar Adrian**, who won the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1932**, supplies biological context.
children: **Neurons are nearly digital**, roughly on or off.
Adrian’s work concerned firing rates, and the sigmoid is a model of a graded activation, not a claim that real neurons have only two states.

teaching.text: **Animal perception** reflects this kind of response.
children: Some things that seem alike are perceived as different, and some things that are very different are perceived as the same.
Inputs on opposite sides of the steep middle can give very different outputs, while inputs near a flat end give nearly the same output.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Sigmoid is applied to the network **one neuron at a time**. The inputs stay **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**, and the weights stay the same.
children: **Purple** neurons are still linear.
**Green** neurons pass their inner product through sigmoid.
The nine hidden neurons are switched in layer order, three, then two, then four.

teaching.text: The first switch changes the first hidden neuron from **−0.400** to about **0.401**.
children: That new output changes what the next layer receives.
Every downstream value is therefore **recalculated**.
This builds a sigmoid network step by step. It is not the same as wrapping sigmoid around the numbers stored from the all-linear network.

teaching.text: After all three first-layer neurons use sigmoid, their outputs are about **0.401, 0.999** and **0.938**.
children: The second layer, recalculated and then passed through sigmoid, gives about **0.713** and **0.223**.
The third layer finishes at about **0.599, 0.609, 0.609** and **0.481**.

teaching.text: The outputs still use **softmax**.
children: With every hidden neuron using sigmoid, **Dan** has the largest probability, about **32.0%**.
**Dean** rises to about **23.0%**, **dune** is about 20.2%, **done** falls to about 16.2% and **Don** is about 8.5%.
The inputs and weights never changed, yet the output pattern did.

teaching.text: This sequence changes the activation rule, not the weights.
children: Dean’s probability is higher than in the all-linear network but still not the largest.
Adding sigmoid can change which word the network favors without showing that the network has learned the right answer.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The PyTorch program is the same as before, with **sigmoid** added to the hidden layers.
children: It still loads **X**, the 110 × 2 formant matrix, and **Y**, the 110 × 5 targets.
**nn.Sigmoid()** now follows **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, **nn.Linear(3, 2)** and **nn.Linear(2, 4)**.

teaching.text: The layer sizes still run **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**.
children: Sigmoid changes each value but not how many values a layer produces.
Three values stay three after sigmoid, so the next **nn.Linear(3, 2)** still receives the right number of inputs.
The same holds for the two-value and four-value hidden layers.

teaching.text: The last layer, **nn.Linear(4, 5)**, has no sigmoid after it.
children: Its five scores are logits for **CrossEntropyLoss**, which handles the softmax-related calculation.
Hidden sigmoid activations and the final word probabilities do different jobs. A hidden neuron is not one of the five words.

teaching.text: The training lines are unchanged.
children: **zero_grad** clears old gradients, the forward pass and loss compare predictions with the targets, **backward** computes gradients and **step** applies the update.
The learning rate is still **0.1**, and all 110 recordings contribute to the single step.

teaching.text: The drawn network uses the original illustrative weights with no biases, where Dan gets **32.0%** and dean **23.0%**.
children: The short program starts with PyTorch’s own default weights and biases.
It matches the drawing’s structure, but reproducing its exact probabilities would also need the same weights and bias settings.
